```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4,
                      message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE,
                      eval = requireNamespace("rms", quietly = TRUE))
```

termeffects draws **simultaneous confidence bands**: bands that are meant to
contain the *whole* true surface, or all true curves, at once with 95%
probability. Ordinary (pointwise) 95% intervals only cover each single point
with 95% probability; over a surface of hundreds of points, some of them will
almost always miss. This vignette reports a simulation study that checks
whether the bands achieve their nominal coverage, for the model types and
interval methods termeffects offers. It is written so that it can serve as
the simulation section of a publication; it is structured following Morris,
White and Crowther (2019) ("ADEMP": aims, data-generating mechanisms,
estimands, methods, performance measures).

The study itself runs for about two hours and is not re-run when this
vignette is built: the code is `validation/11_coverage_study.R` in the
package sources, and its results are stored with the vignette
(`coverage_study_results.csv`).

## Aims

To estimate the coverage probability of termeffects' 95% simultaneous
confidence bands for a non-linear interaction between two continuous
predictors,

* for the main model types: linear regression, logistic regression, Cox
  regression, the proportional odds model (`rms::orm`), and a linear mixed
  model,
* for both interval methods: the analytic band (simulated sup-t critical
  value) and the bootstrap band,
* for a whole prediction surface (heatmap) and for a set of curves (cuts),
* at a small and a moderate sample size,

and to show how far pointwise intervals fall short of covering a whole
surface or set of curves.

## Data-generating mechanisms

**Predictors.** Two focal predictors with standard normal distributions and
correlation 0.4, and one adjustment covariate, also standard normal and
correlated 0.3 with the second:

$$x_1 \sim N(0, 1), \quad x_2 = 0.4\,x_1 + \sqrt{1 - 0.4^2}\,\varepsilon_2, \quad
w = 0.3\,x_2 + \sqrt{1 - 0.3^2}\,\varepsilon_3.$$

**True surface.** The effect of $x_1$ and $x_2$ is a non-linear interaction.
Its true form is defined in two steps. First, a smooth target

$$g(x_1, x_2) = 0.8 \tanh(1.5\,x_1) + 0.4\,x_2 + 0.5 \tanh(x_1)\,x_2 - 0.2\,x_2^2,$$

which levels off in $x_1$, is curved in $x_2$, and in which the effect of
$x_2$ depends on $x_1$. Second, the true surface $f(x_1, x_2)$ is the best
approximation of $g$ (least squares over 200,000 draws of the predictors) by
the model that is fitted later: restricted cubic splines with 4 knots in each
predictor and their full tensor-product interaction,
`rcs(x1, k) * rcs(x2, k)`, with the knots fixed at the 5%, 35%, 65% and 95%
quantiles of the standard normal (the default positions of Harrell, 2015).
The fitted models are therefore correctly specified: the study measures the
inference, not the error of approximating a curve by splines.

```{r truth, fig.height = 3.6, fig.width = 5}
suppressMessages(library(rms))
library(ggplot2)
RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG")
set.seed(20261105)
population <- function(n) {
  x1 <- rnorm(n)
  x2 <- 0.4 * x1 + sqrt(1 - 0.4^2) * rnorm(n)
  w <- 0.3 * x2 + sqrt(1 - 0.3^2) * rnorm(n)
  data.frame(x1 = x1, x2 = x2, w = w)
}
knots <- qnorm(c(0.05, 0.35, 0.65, 0.95))
g <- function(x1, x2) 0.8 * tanh(1.5 * x1) + 0.4 * x2 + 0.5 * tanh(x1) * x2 - 0.2 * x2^2
pop <- population(2e5)
pop$g <- g(pop$x1, pop$x2)
truth_fit <- lm(g ~ rcs(x1, knots) * rcs(x2, knots), data = pop)
q <- qnorm(c(0.05, 0.95))
surface <- expand.grid(x1 = seq(q[1], q[2], length.out = 60), x2 = seq(q[1], q[2], length.out = 60))
surface$f <- predict(truth_fit, surface)
ggplot(surface, aes(x1, x2, fill = f, z = f)) +
  geom_raster() +
  geom_contour(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3, bins = 8) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  labs(x = expression(x[1]), y = expression(x[2]), fill = "f",
       title = "True surface f (central 90% of x1, x2)") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Outcomes.** With linear predictor $\eta = f(x_1, x_2) + 0.5\,w$:

| Model | Outcome | Fitted with |
|:--|:--|:--|
| linear | $y = \eta + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 1)$ | `lm()` |
| logistic | $y \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\text{logit}^{-1}(\eta - 1))$ | `glm(family = binomial)` |
| Cox | event time exponential with hazard $0.1\,e^{\eta}$, censoring uniform on (0, 15) | `survival::coxph()` |
| proportional odds | $y = \eta + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon$ logistic with scale 0.5 (continuous $y$) | `rms::orm()` |
| linear mixed | $y = \eta + u_j + \varepsilon$, clusters $j$ of 10, $u_j \sim N(0, 0.8^2)$, $\varepsilon \sim N(0, 1)$ | `lme4::lmer()`, random intercept |

All models are fitted with the formula `rcs(x1, k) * rcs(x2, k) + w`
(15 coefficients for the interaction surface, plus $w$).

**Sample sizes.** $n$ = 300 and $n$ = 1000. The number of events (logistic,
Cox) is shown with the results.

## Estimands

The true values of the linear predictor (for the proportional odds model:
the mean of $y$) at the points of two grids, with $w$ held at its sample
median, as termeffects does by default:

* **surface**: a 20 × 20 grid over the central 90% of $x_1$ and $x_2$
  (400 points), as shown in a heatmap;
* **curves**: three curves along $x_1$ (30 points each, central 90%), at
  $x_2 = -1, 0, 1$ (90 points), as shown by `term_curves()`.

For the Cox model the estimand is the log hazard ratio relative to the
sample's average covariate vector, which is what `coxph` and termeffects
report. Coverage on the link scale equals coverage on the response scale
(probabilities, hazard ratios), because the bands are transformed with the
same monotone function as the estimates.

## Methods

For each simulated data set the model is fitted and `term_predictions()` is
called with the defaults (95% level, `ci_scope = "global"`, i.e. one band for
the whole grid):

* **Analytic band** (`ci_method = "analytic"`, the default). The critical
  value $c$ is the 95% quantile of $\max_i |Z_i| / \mathrm{SE}_i$ over the grid
  points, where $Z$ is multivariate normal with the covariance of the
  estimated linear predictors, $X V X^\top$ (multivariate $t$ for linear
  models); it is estimated from 5000 simulated draws. The band is
  $\hat\eta_i \pm c\,\mathrm{SE}_i$. This is the sup-t or Working–Hotelling-type
  band (e.g. Ruppert, Wand and Carroll, 2003; Montiel Olea and
  Plagborg-Møller, 2019).
* **Bootstrap band** (`ci_method = "bootstrap"`; not for the mixed model, as
  clusters would have to be resampled). The model is refitted on 500
  resamples of the rows (for `orm`, with `rms::bootcov()`), with the spline
  knots fixed at those of the original fit. $\mathrm{SE}_i$ is the standard
  deviation of the bootstrap predictions, and $c$ is the 95% quantile of
  $\max_i |\hat\eta^*_i - \hat\eta_i| / \mathrm{SE}_i$ over the resamples.
* **Pointwise intervals**, for comparison: $\hat\eta_i \pm 1.96\,\mathrm{SE}_i$
  ($t$ quantile for linear models).

**Number of repetitions.** 1000 data sets per scenario for the analytic
band, and 500 for the bootstrap band (which takes about 500 times longer).
With 1000 repetitions, the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage of 95% is
0.7 percentage points; with 500, 1.0.

## Performance measures

* **Simultaneous coverage**: the proportion of data sets in which the band
  contains the true value at *all* grid points. Target: 95%. Reported with
  its Monte Carlo standard error.
* **Joint coverage of pointwise intervals**: the same, for the pointwise
  intervals; shows what is lost without a simultaneous band.
* **Average pointwise coverage**: the proportion of grid points covered by
  the pointwise intervals, averaged over data sets. Target: 95%; checks the
  standard errors themselves.
* **Critical value**: the average simultaneous critical value, compared with
  1.96, shows how much wider the band is than pointwise intervals.

## Results

```{r results}
res <- read.csv("coverage_study_results.csv")
res$model <- factor(res$outcome, levels = c("linear", "logistic", "cox", "orm", "mixed"),
                    labels = c("Linear", "Logistic", "Cox", "Proportional odds", "Linear mixed"))
res$method <- factor(res$method, levels = c("analytic", "bootstrap"), labels = c("Analytic", "Bootstrap"))
res$estimand <- factor(res$estimand, levels = c("surface", "curves"),
                       labels = c("Surface (400 points)", "Three curves (90 points)"))
```

```{r coverage-plot, fig.height = 5}
ggplot(res, aes(coverage_band, model, colour = factor(n), shape = factor(n))) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.95 - 1.96 * sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / 1000), xmax = 0.95 + 1.96 * sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / 1000),
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey85") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.95, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = coverage_band - 1.96 * mcse_band, xmax = coverage_band + 1.96 * mcse_band),
                 height = 0, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
  facet_grid(method ~ estimand) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("300" = "#E69F00", "1000" = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = function(b) paste0(100 * b, "%")) +
  labs(x = "Simultaneous coverage (with 95% Monte Carlo interval)", y = NULL,
       colour = "n", shape = "n",
       caption = "Dashed: nominal 95%. Grey: range expected by chance with 1000 repetitions.") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

```{r table}
tab <- res[order(res$method, res$estimand, res$model, res$n), ]
pct <- function(p) sprintf("%.1f", 100 * p)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Method = tab$method, Estimand = sub(" \\(.*", "", tab$estimand), Model = tab$model, n = tab$n,
  Events = ifelse(is.na(tab$events), "", sprintf("%.0f", tab$events)),
  Runs = tab$runs,
  `Simultaneous (%)` = paste0(pct(tab$coverage_band), " (", pct(tab$mcse_band), ")"),
  `Pointwise, all points (%)` = pct(tab$coverage_pointwise_all),
  `Pointwise, per point (%)` = pct(tab$coverage_pointwise_mean),
  `Critical value` = sprintf("%.2f", tab$critical_value),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL),
  caption = paste("Coverage of 95% simultaneous bands and pointwise intervals.",
                  "Simultaneous: proportion of data sets in which the band covers the true values at all",
                  "grid points (Monte Carlo standard error). Pointwise, all points: the same for pointwise",
                  "intervals. Pointwise, per point: average proportion of points covered. Events: average",
                  "number of events (logistic, Cox)."))
```

```{r helpers}
raw <- read.csv("coverage_study_results.csv")
cox <- read.csv("coverage_study_cox.csv")
# coverage (in %) of one scenario, e.g. cv("cox", 300, "surface")
cv <- function(outcome, n, estimand, method = "analytic", what = "coverage_band") {
  v <- raw[raw$outcome == outcome & raw$n == n & raw$estimand == estimand & raw$method == method, what]
  sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * v)
}
rng <- function(rows, what = "coverage_band", digits = 1, scale = 100) {
  v <- scale * range(raw[rows, what])
  paste0(sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), v[1]), "–", sprintf(paste0("%.", digits, "f"), v[2]))
}
an <- raw$method == "analytic"
bo <- raw$method == "bootstrap"
failed_analytic <- sum(raw$failed[an & raw$estimand == "surface"])
failed_boot <- sum(raw$failed[bo & raw$estimand == "surface"])
```

### Analytic bands

* **Linear models** reach the nominal level: `r rng(an & raw$outcome == "linear")`%
  over both sample sizes and estimands. This is the case in which the band is
  exact apart from the simulation of the critical value, so it also confirms
  the implementation.
* **Linear mixed models**: `r rng(an & raw$outcome == "mixed")`%: about one
  percentage point below 95% with 30 clusters (n = 300), and at the nominal
  level with 100 clusters.
* **Logistic regression** (`r rng(an & raw$outcome == "logistic", "events", 0, 1)`
  events on average) and the **proportional odds model** are slightly
  conservative: `r rng(an & raw$outcome == "logistic")`% and
  `r rng(an & raw$outcome == "orm")`%.
* **Cox regression** covers less than 95%: for the surface
  `r cv("cox", 300, "surface")` at n = 300 and `r cv("cox", 1000, "surface")`
  at n = 1000, for the curves `r cv("cox", 300, "curves")` and
  `r cv("cox", 1000, "curves")`.

The Cox result needed a closer look: is it a property of the Cox model in
small samples, or an error? A follow-up study
(`validation/12_coverage_cox_sample_size.R`, same data-generating mechanism,
surface estimand, 1000 new data sets per sample size) also recorded the
average standardized error $(\hat\eta_i - \eta_i)/\mathrm{SE}_i$ over the
grid, which should be 0:

```{r cox-follow-up}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  n = cox$n, Events = sprintf("%.0f", cox$events),
  `Events per coefficient` = sprintf("%.0f", cox$events / 16),
  `Mean standardized error (MCSE)` = sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", cox$mean_standardized_error,
                                             cox$mcse_mean_standardized_error),
  `Simultaneous coverage (MCSE)` = sprintf("%.1f%% (%.1f)", 100 * cox$coverage_band, 100 * cox$mcse_band),
  `Pointwise, per point` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cox$coverage_pointwise_mean),
  check.names = FALSE),
  caption = "Cox model, analytic band for the surface, by sample size (16 coefficients).")
```

The estimates lie systematically above the truth, by
`r sprintf("%.2f", cox$mean_standardized_error[1])` standard errors on
average at n = 300. This bias shrinks steadily with n (by a factor of about
two from n = 300 to 1000, and again from 1000 to 4000), as expected for the
small-sample bias of maximum likelihood estimates, which is of order $1/n$
and therefore of order $1/\sqrt{n}$ in units of the standard error (Firth,
1993; Heinze and Schemper, 2001). Coverage rises with it, to
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cox$coverage_band[3])` at n = 4000. An error in
the band's construction would not disappear with growing n. With about 9
events per coefficient (n = 300) the Cox band is too narrow; with about 30 it
is close to, but still below, the nominal level. (At n = 300 the two studies
estimate the surface coverage as `r cv("cox", 300, "surface")` and
`r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * cox$coverage_band[1])`; the difference is about
two Monte Carlo standard errors.)

### Bootstrap bands

The bootstrap bands are **conservative**: for logistic and Cox regression
they covered the truth in
`r rng(bo & raw$outcome %in% c("logistic", "cox"))`% of data sets, with
critical values of
`r rng(bo & raw$outcome %in% c("logistic", "cox"), "critical_value", 2, 1)`
instead of about 3.0–3.3 for the analytic bands, and even the pointwise intervals built from the
bootstrap standard errors covered more than 95% of points
(`r rng(bo & raw$outcome %in% c("logistic", "cox"), "coverage_pointwise_mean")`%).
In resamples, sparse regions of the grid occasionally get extreme estimates
(e.g. near-separation in logistic regression), which inflates both the
bootstrap standard errors and the maximum over the grid. The effect is
largest at n = 300 and smaller at n = 1000. For linear and proportional odds
models the bootstrap bands are close to nominal or slightly conservative
(`r rng(bo & raw$outcome %in% c("linear", "orm"))`%). The bootstrap
therefore did not give too narrow bands, but often much wider ones than
needed; the analytic band is preferable, and the bootstrap is useful as a
check where the model's own standard errors are in doubt.

### Pointwise intervals

Pointwise 95% intervals covered about 95% of the points each
(`r rng(an, "coverage_pointwise_mean")`% per point for the analytic
intervals), but contained the whole true surface in only
`r rng(an & raw$estimand == "surface", "coverage_pointwise_all", 0)`% of data
sets, and all three curves in
`r rng(an & raw$estimand == "curves", "coverage_pointwise_all", 0)`%. Reading
a heatmap or a set of curves with pointwise intervals therefore overstates
the precision of the shape. The simultaneous critical values were about
`r rng(an & raw$estimand == "surface", "critical_value", 1, 1)` for the
surface and `r rng(an & raw$estimand == "curves", "critical_value", 1, 1)` for
the curves, i.e. the simultaneous bands are about 1.5–1.7 times as wide as
pointwise intervals.

### Failed fits

`rms::orm()` did not converge in `r failed_analytic` of 2000 data sets
(analytic scenarios) and `r failed_boot` of 1000 (bootstrap scenarios); these
data sets are excluded. All other fits succeeded.

## Conclusions

* termeffects' analytic simultaneous bands achieve their nominal 95%
  coverage for linear and linear mixed models, and are slightly conservative
  for logistic and proportional odds models, both for whole surfaces and for
  sets of curves.
* For Cox models with few events per coefficient the bands are too narrow,
  because of the small-sample bias of the Cox estimates; coverage approaches
  95% as the number of events grows. With complex spline interactions in Cox
  models, plan for many events, or read the bands as approximate.
* Bootstrap bands never under-covered here but were often much wider than
  needed, especially for logistic and Cox models at n = 300.
* Pointwise intervals cover the whole surface far less often than 95%;
  simultaneous bands are needed to read the shape of a surface or to compare
  curves.

**Limitations.** One data-generating mechanism (one true surface, two
correlated normal predictors), correctly specified models with prespecified
knots (data-driven knot choice and model selection are not part of the
inference), grids restricted to the central 90% of each predictor, two
sample sizes (three for Cox), and random-intercept models only. Coverage in
regions with very few observations, e.g. corners of a heatmap outside the
bulk of the data, may be worse than reported here.


## Reproducing the study

```r
# from the package source folder; about 2 hours on 7 cores
Sys.setenv(OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS = 1)   # or set it before starting R
source("validation/11_coverage_study.R")
```

The script writes the per-run results to
`validation/output/11_coverage_runs.csv`, any failed fits to
`validation/output/11_coverage_failures.csv`, the R session information to
`validation/output/11_session_info.txt`, and the summary used here to
`vignettes/coverage_study_results.csv`. The Cox follow-up is
`validation/12_coverage_cox_sample_size.R` (about 15 minutes), which writes
`vignettes/coverage_study_cox.csv`.

## References

Harrell FE (2015). *Regression Modeling Strategies*, 2nd ed. Springer.

Montiel Olea JL, Plagborg-Møller M (2019). Simultaneous confidence bands:
theory, implementation, and an application to SVARs. *Journal of Applied
Econometrics* 34:1–17.

Morris TP, White IR, Crowther MJ (2019). Using simulation studies to evaluate
statistical methods. *Statistics in Medicine* 38:2074–2102.

Ruppert D, Wand MP, Carroll RJ (2003). *Semiparametric Regression*.
Cambridge University Press.

Firth D (1993). Bias reduction of maximum likelihood estimates. *Biometrika*
80:27–38.

Heinze G, Schemper M (2001). A solution to the problem of monotone likelihood
in Cox regression. *Biometrics* 57:114–119.
